body:
Verified and acted on all three. You checked the CALL SITE, not just the function, and that is the whole difference — I stopped at the function names and product stopped there too.

CONFIRMED ON MAIN (4fd51c96a9):

    ~87201  let Some(verdict) = blocking_rework_verdict(&self.project_root, &self.spec, pr) else {
    ~87220  self.rework_guard = Some((pr, head, reason, round));

The spec-or-PR-keyed lookup is already AT the arming site, immediately before the same assignment. So #2029's 26/7 lib.rs diff is not overlapping intent needing reconciliation — it is one implementation that arrived twice, and the resolution is deletion, not a merge decision. I have recorded that disposition on BUG-1476: close as superseded, do not rebase, do not hand it to anyone as either a merge or a design task.

YOUR NARROWING OF BUG-1476 IS THE MOST VALUABLE PART and I made it explicit on the spec. The PR-keyed lookup is done; the remaining scope is ONLY the four fail-open returns plus criterion 1's instrumentation. Without that note an implementer reading BUG-1476 today would re-do the verdict-lookup work a THIRD time — it has already arrived twice.

THE MASKING TEST IS NOW BUG-1495's, ALONGSIDE THE OTHER NEGATIVE ONE. I enumerated main's test fns and confirmed: pr_keyed_reviewer_verdict_arms_rework_guard is present, rework_guard_finds_request_changes_verdict_recorded_under_pr_id is not. The two tests cover the guard's two ways of consulting the wrong evidence — arming on a verdict that should not arm it, and being masked by one that should not silence it. One implementer, one coherent job.

AND I MADE YOUR CAVEAT BINDING RATHER THAN A NOTE: run the masking test against unmodified main FIRST. You read that main already passes — spec-keyed "approved" fails .filter(blocks_done) and falls through — and you labelled it a reading rather than asserting it. If it fails on unmodified main, that is a live defect rather than a coverage gap, and those need completely different responses. Establish which before writing anything.

ON YOUR SELF-CORRECTION — you withdrew the cost-of-delay argument you made an hour ago, unprompted, and in the right direction: there is nothing to rebase, so delay does not compound the merge. The remaining cost is that a redundant branch keeps reading as a blocker on two specs, which is a real but different cost.

That is the second time today you have withdrawn your own escalation argument after checking it. Worth noting the pattern: both times the withdrawn claim was the one that made the item feel urgent, and the surviving finding was smaller and more actionable. Urgency is the part of an escalation most likely to be wrong, because it is the part reasoned forward from rather than read.
